newsitem.title: USA: Asian workers abused on Mariana Islands - report.
newsitem.headline: Asian workers abused on Mariana Islands - report.

text.p: Thousands of Asian workers are exploited and abused in the U.S. territory of the Northern Mariana Islands, a senior House of Representatives Democrat charged on Thursday.

"Today I am releasing a major report that documents the systematic, persistent and inexcusable exploitation of men and women in sweatshops in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands," Representative George Miller of California said.

The report by the Democratic staff of the House Resources Committee found that workers were brought from the Philippines, South Korea, China, Japan, Palau and Micronesia to the Mariana Islands to work in crowded garment shops.

Asian women recruited to work as waitresses in the territory were forced to become prostitutes or nude dancers when they arrived. "Women who refuse are kidnapped, raped and tortured," the report said.

The United States captured the 14 islands that make up the Northern Mariana Islands from Japan during the Second World War. In 1975, residents of the islands voted to become a commonwealth under the sovereignty of the United States, making them U.S. citizens.

Washington gave the commonwealth control to enforce U.S. immigration and minimum wage laws, but the report charged that the laws were ignored. Foreign workers and their children now outnumber U.S. citizens among the 58,800 residents of the islands.
Garment workers in the islands get an average of $2.90 an hour, compared with the U.S. minimum wage of $4.75 an hour. Farmers and household workers get even less.
The commonwealth government in Saipan also ignored U.S. laws allowing workers to unionize and fails to aggressively prosecute those who mistreat foreign workers, the report said.

Miller introduced legislation to increase the minimum wage until it matches the federal rate and to bring immigration laws under control of the U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service. His bill would also prohibit use of the "Made in the USA" label on clothing made in the islands unless companies obeyed all U.S. labour laws.

Juan Babauta, the commonwealth's representative in Washington, said he had not seen the legislation. But in a letter to Miller on Tuesday, he said, "I have previously testified that local control of minimum wage and immigration can and should be managed responsibly by local authorities."
